extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy; readers of John Locke; general educated readers interested in empiricism and theory of ideas
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and analysis of Locke's account of how the mind forms and classifies ideas, especially the origin of ideas (sensation and reflection) and the taxonomy of complex ideas (modes, substances, relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: examine faculties via simple ideas first
rubrics_metrics.description: These, I think, are the first faculties and operations of the mind, which it makes use of in understanding ... I have subjoined the explication of these faculties of the mind to that of simple ideas, before I come to what I have to say concerning complex ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: (1) Several faculties are exercised at first principally about simple ideas so we may trace them in their rise and gradual improvements; (2) simple ideas are usually clearer/precise than complex ones so observing faculties on simple ideas helps examine how mind forms complex ideas; (3) operations about ideas received from sensations are themselves another set of ideas (reflection) fit to be considered after simple ideas. Use following treatment when analyzing or presenting mental faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: True beginning of human knowledge — appeal to experience
rubrics_metrics.description: A short, and, I think, true HISTORY OF THE FIRST BEGINNINGS OF HUMAN KNOWLEDGE;—whence the mind has its first objects; and by what steps it makes its progress ... the best way to come to truth being to examine things as really they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological criterion: appeal to experience and observation to test claims about origins of ideas; do not posit innate ideas or infused principles without experiential warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to experience as sole discoverable source
rubrics_metrics.description: To deal truly, this is the only way that I can discover, whereby the IDEAS OF THINGS are brought into the understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit stance: if others claim innate ideas they may keep them, but the speaker can only report what is found by experience and reflection. Use experiential examples across ages, countries, and educations to test universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: External and internal sensation are the only passages of knowledge (Dark Room)
rubrics_metrics.description: I pretend not to teach, but to inquire; and therefore cannot but confess here again,—that external and internal sensation are the only passages I can find of knowledge to the understanding. These alone ... are the windows by which light is let into this DARK ROOM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: treat the understanding as a closet shut from light except for small openings; when explaining origins of ideas, foreground senses (sight, touch) and reflection as the two channels for ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas are made by the mind out of simple ones
rubrics_metrics.description: As simple ideas are observed to exist in several combinations united together, so the mind has a power to consider several of them united together as one idea ... Ideas thus made up of several simple ones put together, I call COMPLEX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical rule: when accounting for any complex idea, show how it is composed (voluntarily or by observation) from simple ideas received from sensation and reflection; emphasize mind's creativity but limit compositions to available simple ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on origin of ideas: no ideas beyond sensation/reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: But all this still confined to those simple ideas which it received from those two sources, and which are the ultimate materials of all its compositions. For simple ideas are all from things themselves, and of these the mind CAN have no more, nor other than what are suggested to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for evaluating claims about concepts: demand lineage to sensation or reflection; reject purported ideas that lack such origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of complex ideas: Modes, Substances, Relations
rubrics_metrics.description: COMPLEX IDEAS ... may be all reduced under these three heads:—1. MODES. 2. SUBSTANCES. 3. RELATIONS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying complex ideas, place them under the appropriate head and justify by showing whether they presuppose subsisting by themselves (substance), are affections/dependences of substances (modes), or are comparative (relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes: dependent complex ideas (simple modes and mixed modes)
rubrics_metrics.description: MODES I call such complex ideas which ... are considered as dependences on, or affections of substances ... Of these MODES, there are two sorts: First, simple modes ... variations or different combinations of the same simple idea ... Secondly, mixed modes ... compounded of simple ideas of several kinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between simple modes (repetitions/variations of one simple idea like a dozen) and mixed modes (combinations of different simple ideas like beauty or theft). Provide examples when analyzing or teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substances: ideas representing particulars, single or collective
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideas of SUBSTANCES are such combinations of simple ideas as are taken to represent distinct PARTICULAR things subsisting by themselves ... there are two sorts of ideas:—one of SINGLE substances ... the other of several of those put together ... COLLECTIVE ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To identify a substance-idea, show the 'supposed or confused idea of substance' joined to particular sensible qualities; note examples (lead, man, army) and the distinction between individual and collective substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations: complex ideas consisting in comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The last sort of complex ideas is that we call RELATION, which consists in the consideration and comparing one idea with another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating relational ideas, emphasize the act of comparison as constitutive; provide comparative examples and show how relations derive from simpler ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even the most abstruse ideas derive from sensation or reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: EVEN THE MOST ABSTRUSE IDEAS, how remote soever they may seem from sense, or from any operations of our own minds, are yet only such as the understanding frames to itself, by repeating and joining together ideas that it had either from objects of sense, or from its own operations about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic demand: for abstract concepts (space, time, infinity) demonstrate their derivation by showing the process of repeating/joining simple ideas; use this as a touchstone against claims of purely innate abstract knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of space arises from sight and touch; distinctions: distance, capacity, extension
rubrics_metrics.description: We get the idea of space, both by our sight and touch ... This space, considered barely in length between any two beings ... is called DISTANCE: if considered in length, breadth, and thickness ... CAPACITY. When considered between the extremities of matter ... it is properly called EXTENSION.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing 'space' or teaching it, distinguish rigorously between distance (space), capacity, and extension (affection of body); use sensory examples (sight, touch) to ground the explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place as a relative modification of space determined by purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Another idea coming under this head ... is that we call PLACE. ... men consider and determine of this place by reference to those adjacent things which best served to their present purpose ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain 'place' by showing how it is defined relative to chosen reference points for a given purpose (examples: chessboard, book/verse location, ship vs earth). Emphasize purposive selection of reference frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space is distinct from extension and body (arguments given)
rubrics_metrics.description: I think it most intelligible ... if we use the word extension for an affection of matter ... and space in the more general signification, for distance, with or without solid matter possessing it ... SPACE and SOLIDITY being as distinct ideas as THINKING and EXTENSION.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support distinction with several arguments presented: (1) extension excludes solidity/resistance; (2) parts of pure space are inseparable and immovable; (3) the definition of extension is circular; (4) conceivability of vacuum and annihilation show separability. Use these criteria when evaluating claims that conflate space and body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of vacuum (space without body) — multiple arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: For vacuum, whether we affirm or deny its existence, signifies space without body ... If God placed a man at the extremity of corporeal beings, he could stretch his hand beyond his body ... the motion of bodies ... seems to me plainly to evince it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments offered: (a) divine annihilation thought-experiment (space remains after matter removed); (b) motion and division of matter require void to allow parts to move; (c) conceivability of space without body suffices to have the idea. Use these when assessing metaphysical claims about plenitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about the word 'substance'—ambiguity and limited epistemic role
rubrics_metrics.description: If it be demanded whether this space, void of body, be SUBSTANCE or ACCIDENT, I shall readily answer I know not ... Names made at pleasure, neither alter the nature of things, nor make us understand them ... the word substance would have done it effectually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical recommendation: avoid conflating multiple senses of 'substance'; require clear, distinct ideas before using the term as an explanatory principle; be wary of treating 'substance' as informative rather than a placeholder for ignorance.
